rows.title: The wheel's many reinventions
rows.standfirst: "Don't reinvent the wheel" is a common phrase, but structural engineer Roma Agrawal doesn't buy it.

rows.title: Advertiser backlash may pose mortal threat to Elon Musk's X
rows.standfirst: Advertising insiders say their clients are worried about the fallout if they place ads on X.

rows.title: CosMc's lands in Illinois, as McDonald's tests its new coffee-centered concept
rows.standfirst: The beverage-first McDonald's spinoff, named for a six-handed extraterrestrial, seems to be a grab at markets currently served by the likes of Starbucks and Dunkin' Donuts.

rows.title: White House proposes to 'march in' on patents for costly drugs
rows.standfirst: To lower drug prices, the Biden administration is looking to assert its authority to license drug patents that rely on government-funded research to drugmakers that would offer cheaper medicines.

rows.title: 'Washington Post' journalists stage daylong strike under threat of job cuts
rows.standfirst: Workers are on a 24-hour strike to pressure owner Jeff Bezos and company leaders to negotiate a new labor contract. The Post says it needs to cut jobs and may resort to layoffs.

rows.title: A record number of fossil fuel representatives are at this year's COP28 climate talks
rows.standfirst: With a record number of oil, gas and coal representatives at this year's COP28 climate talks, climate scientists worry industry influence could water down language on fossil fuels.

rows.title: What can we learn from the year's most popular econ terms?
rows.standfirst: In 2021, the most popular term on Investopedia was "capital gains tax." In 2022, it was "poison pill." These top terms help capture the economic zeitgeist of their year. So... what was it in 2023?

rows.title: Two food and drink indicators
rows.standfirst: Today on the show, we have two episodes from our daily podcast, The Indicator, about things we spend a lot of time thinking about this time of year: food and drink.

rows.title: 'Time' magazine names Taylor Swift its 2023 Person of the Year
rows.standfirst: The 33-year-old international pop star has been playing to massive crowds on her Eras Tour and has garnered attention for her budding romance with Kansas City Chiefs tight end Travis Kelce.

rows.title: Americans don't like higher prices but they LOVE buying new things
rows.standfirst: Eight times a year, regional Federal Reserve Banks release a collection of anecdotes that reveal stories about the economy. These stories come together in what's known as the "Beige Book," and we award the regional bank with the best entry with our coveted Beigie Award. Today, we're highlighting an entry that gets to the heart of the contradictions we're seeing when it comes to consumer preferences and sentiment.

rows.title: Supreme Court seems inclined to leave major offshore tax in place on investors
rows.standfirst: An eventual decision in the case could severely limit congressional options in enacting tax policy, and it could cost the federal government trillions of dollars in corporate taxes.

rows.title: Oil companies are embracing terms like 'lower carbon.' Here's what they really mean
rows.standfirst: The oil industry has a huge voice in this year's climate talks. But what are oil companies actually saying? And why does it matter? We break down their pledges and statements into plain English.

rows.title: The U.S. supports China's growth if it 'plays by the rules,' commerce secretary says
rows.standfirst: China's president says success for the U.S. and China can be mutually beneficial. U.S. Commerce Secretary Gina Raimondo says that the reality is a bit more complicated than that.

rows.title: Ex-British officials say Murdoch tabloids hacked them to aid corporate agenda
rows.standfirst: Ex-U.K. cabinet ministers allege Murdoch's tabloids hacked their voicemails for salacious scoops to try to intimidate them from blocking its takeover of a satellite TV firm.

rows.title: Supreme Court hears a case that experts say could wreak havoc on the tax code
rows.standfirst: A couple who owned a controlling interest in a foreign corporation argue that a controversial Trump-era tax is unconstitutional under the 16th Amendment.

rows.title: What women want (to invest in)
rows.standfirst: Women lag behind men when it comes to investing. Combine this with the fact that women tend to earn less than their male peers and live longer, and it can create a waterfall of awful long-term consequences for half of America's population. Today, we speak to an author of an investing study who says he's found a solution.

rows.title: Tribes celebrate historic deal with White House that could save Pacific Northwest salmon
rows.standfirst: The White House has reached what it says is an historic agreement over the restoration of salmon in the Pacific Northwest, a deal that could end for now a decades long legal battle with tribes.

rows.title: 'Shameless': Reporters Without Borders rebukes X for claiming to support it
rows.standfirst: X recently claimed to support the press advocacy group Reporters Without Borders — which in response called X "a haven for disinformation."

rows.title: Broken wings: Complaints about U.S. airlines soared again this year
rows.standfirst: Passenger complaints about airlines rose sharply in the first half of the year, according to consumer watchdogs. The number of canceled flights declined, but delays and other problems increased.

rows.title: Cobalt is in demand, so why did America's only cobalt mine close?
rows.standfirst: America's only cobalt mine opened last year to great fanfare, since the mineral is crucial for green energy. But it surprisingly closed months later.

rows.title: Why '90s ads are unforgettable
rows.standfirst: Maybe she's born with it, maybe it's __________.

rows.title: The 'physics' behind potential interest rate cuts
rows.standfirst: In the world of science there are laws—rules that describe how the universe works. The Federal Reserve has its own set of rules, except its rules are more like guidelines to help the Fed decide where interest rates should be. Today on the show, we explain inertial and non-inertial rules in the world of monetary policy, and what they tell us about potential rate cuts in the year ahead.

rows.title: The Fed is probably done raising interest rates and could cut them next year
rows.standfirst: The Federal Reserve held interest rates steady on Wednesday, amid signs of easing inflation. The central bank signaled that its benchmark borrowing rate may start to fall next year.

rows.title: Epic Games beat Google but lost to Apple in monopoly lawsuits. What does it all mean?
rows.standfirst: The tech giants' app stores are multibillion-dollar money-makers. Now the services are under threat like never before.

rows.title: Tesla recalls over 2 million vehicles to fix defective Autopilot monitoring system
rows.standfirst: The recall comes after a two-year investigation by the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration into a series of crashes — some deadly — that happened while the Autopilot system was in use.

rows.title: Wall Street calls them 'the Magnificent 7': They're the reason why stocks are surging
rows.standfirst: The S&P 500 has surged this year, but most of those gains are thanks to a handful companies nicknamed "the Magnificent Seven." And that's worrying Wall Street.

rows.title: Why it's so hard to resist holiday sales (and how to try)
rows.standfirst: Malls are designed to overwhelm our brains. Add the stress of holiday shopping, and a quick trip to pick up presents could turn into an hours-long shopping spree thanks to all the ways stores use research from fields like consumer neuroscience and neuromarketing to entice you. Retailers create urgency and scarcity to push you to give into the emotional part of your brain, motivated by the release of dopamine.

rows.title: Are the products in your shopping cart real?
rows.standfirst: How often are you shopping online and think to yourself, is that shirt/dress/jeans in my shopping cart ... even real? That is a question some shoppers are asking themselves as AI-generated products increasingly infiltrate the world of e-commerce.

rows.title: Broken promise – A VA fix to a home-loan crisis exposed by NPR is leaving thousands of veterans in danger of losing their homes
rows.standfirst: An NPR investigation reveals thousands of veterans on the brink of foreclosure, through no fault of their own, after a blunder at the Department of Veterans Affairs.

rows.title: Zara pulls ad campaign that critics said resembled Gaza destruction
rows.standfirst: The multinational fashion retailer Zara said it regrets a "misunderstanding" about its latest ad campaign after public outcry over images that some said evoked the war in Gaza.

rows.title: The 'Yellowstone' effect on Montana
rows.standfirst: Yellowstone first aired in 2018, quickly becoming one of television's most popular shows. The show follows John Dutton, played by Kevin Costner, as he feuds with real estate developers threatening to encroach on his family ranch. Today on the show, how life imitates art in Montana, where tourism has boomed, the population has grown and housing prices have soared.

rows.title: More than 2.5 million Honda and Acura vehicles are recalled for a fuel pump defect
rows.standfirst: Honda Motor's American arm is recalling more than 2.5 million vehicles in the U.S. due to a fuel pump defect that can increase risks of engine failure or stalling while driving.

rows.title: After 38 years on the job, Santa Luke still has time for everyone. Yes, you too
rows.standfirst: We spent a day soaking up the low-key magic made by Luke "Santa Luke" Durant, who draws large crowds — young and old — to storied Mondawmin Mall in Baltimore.

rows.title: How a utility company fought to keep two Colorado towns hooked on fossil fuels
rows.standfirst: Environmental advocates worry natural gas providers are using customer dollars to block local action on climate change. Colorado is one of a handful of states trying to limit the practice.

rows.title: Tweens used to hate showers. Now, they're taking over Sephora
rows.standfirst: Holiday wish lists are all dewy skin drops, hyaluronic acid and lip oil — leaving parents amused and confused.

rows.title: Dollarizing Argentina
rows.standfirst: Argentina has been on a decades-long search for economic stability, but it always seems to be out of reach. High inflation has been plaguing the country and just surpassed 160% a year.

rows.title: States are trashing troves of masks and protective gear as costly stockpiles expire
rows.standfirst: As a deadline to allocate federal COVID-19 cash approaches next year, states must decide how much to invest in maintaining warehouses and supply stockpiles after panic buying during the pandemic.

rows.title: How economics can help you stick to your New Year's resolution
rows.standfirst: Talk of New Year's resolutions is bubbling up as 2024 quickly approaches. Whether it's a fitness goal, wanting to learn a new skill or just trying to develop better habits, a new year is the perfect excuse to start. However, it can be difficult to maintain as time passes by.

rows.title: Toyota recalls 1 million vehicles for defect that may prevent air bags from deploying
rows.standfirst: Toyota said a defect could cause airbags not to deploy, increasing the risk of injury. The vehicles include Avalons, Camrys, Highlanders, RAV4s, Siennas and Corollas for model years 2020 to 2022.

rows.title: New 'Washington Post' CEO accused of Murdoch tabloid hacking cover-up
rows.standfirst: Lawyers for Prince Harry and Hugh Grant have alleged in court that The Washington Post 's next CEO helped the Murdochs clean up after illegal phone-hacking incidents at their British tabloids.

rows.title: Coyote vs. Warner Bros. Discovery
rows.standfirst: The movie Coyote vs. Acme was set to release this summer featuring characters from the iconic Looney Tunes cartoons. The studio behind the film, Warner Bros. Pictures, had some other ideas. Instead of releasing the completed film, the studio canceled Coyote vs. Acme, with no intention of ever releasing it.

rows.title: A look back at some of the biggest and weirdest auctions of 2023
rows.standfirst: An unopened first-generation iPhone. A rundown property with an unbeatable view. Pachyderms. Here's a recap of this year in auction highlights, as told by NPR.

rows.title: Biden has big plans for semiconductors. But there's a big hole: not enough workers
rows.standfirst: President Biden has $52.7 billion to invest in U.S. semiconductor manufacturing plants. But there's a big shortfall in workers for the new jobs.

rows.title: Google to pay $700 million in case over whether its app store is an illegal monopoly
rows.standfirst: The deal with dozens of states resolves a lawsuit that claimed Google engages in anticompetitive behavior through its Google Play store, which is how most people download apps on Android devices.

rows.title: Apple stops selling latest Apple Watch after losing patent case
rows.standfirst: Apple said sales of its Series 9 and Ultra 2 smartwatches would be halted this week after it lost a case over whether the tech giant stole a patented blood oxygen feature from another company.

rows.title: Driverless car startup Cruise's no good, terrible year
rows.standfirst: After rapidly expanding its self-driving car program, things took a disastrous turn for Cruise when one of its robotaxis struck a pedestrian.

rows.title: Google settles $5 billion privacy lawsuit over tracking people using 'incognito mode'
rows.standfirst: The class-action lawsuit said Google misled users into believing that it wouldn't track their internet activities while using 'incognito mode.' Terms of the settlement weren't disclosed.

rows.title: The Rest of the Story, 2023
rows.standfirst: It's that time of year again! Our annual year-end tradition of checking in on the stories we've reported and the people we met along the way.

rows.title: First edible mascot in sports history stars in the Pop-Tarts Bowl
rows.standfirst: Kansas State beat NC State, 28-19, after which the winning team devoured the giant pastry that emerged from an even more giant toaster in what was a clever marketing move.

rows.title: Boeing urges airlines to check its 737 Max jets for loose bolts
rows.standfirst: The FAA says it's closely monitoring the Boeing-requested checks after an unnamed international airline discovered a bolt with a missing nut on a 737 Max while performing routine maintenance.

rows.title: Chasing the American Dream at Outback Steakhouse (Classic)
rows.standfirst: How often do you hang out with people in a different socioeconomic bracket than you? And where do you meet and congregate? Economist Maxim Massenkoff, and his co-author Nathan Wilmers, looked at cell phone location data to figure out where people with vastly different incomes commune together. Today on the show, Maxim discusses his research, and Darian and Alexi head to a restaurant to try and witness some of this class mixing in action.

rows.title: AMC Theatres apologizes for kicking out a civil rights leader for using his own chair
rows.standfirst: Bishop William J. Barber II, who suffers from a chronic and painful form of arthritis, was escorted out of an AMC movie theater after he tried to use his own chair in the accessible section.

rows.title: 'Let's Get It On' ... in court (Update)
rows.standfirst: *This episode originally aired on April 20th, 2023*

rows.title: Why corporate bankruptcies were up in 2023 despite the improving economy
rows.standfirst: Hundreds of debt-saddled companies filed for bankruptcy this year, as the era of easy money caught up to corporations. High interest rates mean banks aren't extending lifelines.

rows.title: How rock-bottom prices drive shortages of generic drugs used in hospitals
rows.standfirst: Hospitals rely on scores of generic drugs given by injection. But these workhorses are often in short supply. Cheap prices have led to factory closures that leave the supply chain vulnerable.

rows.title: The $7,500 tax credit for electric cars keeps changing. Here's how to get it now
rows.standfirst: The IRS has made it a bit easier for EVs to qualify for tax credits in 2025. In the meantime, here's what you need to know about which cars are eligible right now.

rows.title: U.S. appeals court grants Apple's request to pause smartwatch import ban
rows.standfirst: The stay temporarily halts an import ban on some watches as Apple appeals a U.S. International Trade Commission ruling that it infringed on the patents of medical technology company Masimo.

rows.title: A lesson in Barbie labor economics (Classic)
rows.standfirst: *This episode originally aired on July 24th, 2023*

rows.title: 'New York Times' sues ChatGPT creator OpenAI, Microsoft, for copyright infringement
rows.standfirst: The Times is the first major news publisher to take OpenAI to court over the use of its copyright material in its popular chatbot. The suit follows months of tense negotiations between the two sides.

rows.title: These 5 charts show how life got pricier, but also cheaper, in 2023
rows.standfirst: Inflation eased this year, and wages are now climbing faster than prices. Americans are still spending, even if they have to borrow money to do so.
